items.title: Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist
items.summary: The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3.
items.body: Consumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections , with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool. The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October and much better than the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 92.2. Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly. Still, confidence among Republicans remained the highest among the three groups. While respondents "continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs," they also "cited hope for the general economy," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators.

items.title: AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns
items.summary: Fears about some companies' AI debt ramped higher Tuesday, a day after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.
items.body: Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom. Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors. CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points.

items.title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away

items.body: Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month. The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return. Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology. President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

items.title: Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return
items.summary: US president says he ‘convinced’ chipmaker’s board to reinstate CEO, as Nvidia shares fall after previous day’s rally Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive? Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US…
items.body: Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive . Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from the US president. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.” The US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times. Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% on Monday, adding about $950bn to the company’s value.

items.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
items.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.
items.body: The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks. After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher. The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported. The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year.

items.title: Boris Vujčić: Resilience in an age of shocks: lessons from central and eastern Europe
items.body: Yet the same openness that enabled convergence has also exposed CEE countries to repeated shocks. In the space of just a few years, Europe has faced a pandemic, Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine, an unprecedented energy shock, disruptions to global supply chains and, more recently, renewed trade tensions and conflict in the Middle East. These developments have placed economic resilience at the centre of the policy debate. And central and eastern Europe provides a particularly useful lens through which to think about what resilience means. The experience of CEE economies provides valuable lessons for Europe as a whole. It shows us that openness and resilience are not opposites. In fact, integration can be a source of resilience through diversifying markets, suppliers and sources of financing.

items.title: Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
items.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done. Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you," Huang said, according to one of the people. The CEO also addressed succession planning during the event, the people said. He told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.

items.title: Why France is at risk of recession — and what could keep it out of one
items.summary: Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin told CNBC he still expects growth, pointing to resilience in sectors including defense, aerospace and electricity.
items.body: France's economy is flashing fresh recession warnings as businesses delay decisions ahead of the 2027 election — but resilient industries, progress on the budget and lower energy costs could help keep growth positive. Business activity declined to a six-month low in November, with manufacturing performing worse than the services sector, according to the S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index published on Monday. The French private sector is at its most pessimistic about the coming year since late 2012, excluding the months at the start of the pandemic, according to the survey, with job losses recorded for a seventh straight month. Among the biggest challenges cited by companies were economic conditions, uncertainty, competition and cost pressures, while frail domestic demand is weighing on sales.

items.title: Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets
items.summary: The product, the first one beyond event contracts, was introduced in May.
items.body: Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports , politics and culture . But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days. On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off . That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day. Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market.

Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk. "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse. Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia." items.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
items.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
items.body: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17. Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US. In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation. In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".

items.title: Irish plan offers Burnham breakthrough on Made in Europe
items.summary: Irish presidency of EU proposes giving UK ‘partner’ status on assembly of cars in possible boost to reset of relations The UK would not have to follow the EU and apply tariffs on Chinese car imports under an Irish proposal that could prove another breakthrough for the prime…
items.body: The UK would not have to follow the EU and apply tariffs on Chinese car imports under an Irish proposal that could prove another breakthrough for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, in his reset of relations with the bloc. The proposal comes as the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told a parliamentary committee that there had been “a transformation in the EU view”. Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency and plays a central role in steering legislation, has come up with a compromise under which the UK would be included in the bloc’s new “Made in Europe” legislation without having to align with the EU’s trade policies. Made in Europe , or the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is designed to protect the bloc’s supply chains from cheap competition, mainly from China, particularly in the automotive and clean energy sectors.

items.title: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years
items.summary: Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.
items.body: Insmed shares rallied 14% on Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023. The proposed acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash. It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff , when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023. Insmed shares closed up 14.1% at $170.15 on Tuesday, while Sanofi stock closed up 10.9% in Paris.

items.title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
items.summary: Here is what you need to know about the payment that millions will receive from January.
items.body: Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget. For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context. A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January , according to consultants Cornwall Insight. Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said. As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in , external . If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box. The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.

items.body: Evgeny Lebedev, the son of a Russian billionaire and owner of the Standard newspaper, has cut £5m off the asking price for his London mansion. The eight-bedroom Grade II-listed house sits on the Hampton Court estate, a former hunting ground of King Henry VIII on the south-west edge of London . It was first listed in July for £25m, but that has been reduced to £19.85m. Prices have dropped sharply in some of London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods such as Belgravia and Knightsbridge, amid a broader slowdown in the capital’s luxury property market . Many wealthy international buyers are thought to have been put off by the end of the non-dom regime as well as higher property taxes. Even with the £5m reduction, which was first reported by the Telegraph, the purchase could trigger a stamp duty charge of as much as £3m.

items.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
items.body: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy. The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump. Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers. But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market. Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.

items.title: Channel 4 hit as Unilever switches from TV to influencer marketing
items.summary: Exclusive: Gogglebox broadcaster is bigger loser than its rivals after Dove owner’s strategy shift, analysis shows Channel 4 has suffered a blow after one of Britain’s biggest advertisers ditched almost all of its TV spending with the troubled broadcaster, in favour of a switch…
items.body: Channel 4 has suffered a blow after one of Britain’s biggest advertisers ditched almost all of its TV spending with the troubled broadcaster, in favour of a switch to online influencer marketing. Unilever, the owner of brands including Dove soap and Hellmann’s mayonnaise, has cut down its almost £100m UK TV advertising budget, with Channel 4 the biggest victim. Analysis for the Guardian by industry sources shows Unilever’s UK TV media spend has plummeted by just over 50% so far this year compared with 2025. The Anglo-Dutch company has traditionally been a top-three TV advertiser in the UK, alongside Procter & Gamble and the Sky parent company, Comcast. According to the figures, Channel 4 has been the hardest hit proportionally, with Unilever slashing approximately 92% of its spending with the broadcaster, which is making record swingeing job cuts amid a tough advertising market.

items.title: How Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent
items.summary: Meta doesn't serve ads in its Muse personal agent, but the tool is already boosting the company's ad business, a senior executive told CNBC.
items.body: Meta' s ad-free Muse personal artificial intelligence agent is already helping the social media giant boost its advertising business, and it's happening through Instagram, multiple people told CNBC. Instagram is a major advertising revenue engine for the social media giant, and the company is leveraging existing habits on the platform by prompting users to organize their saved posts in Muse. About 20% of daily Instagram users save at least one post to the app per day, according to a person familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because the information is not public. Many of those saved items, the person said, are either shoppable items or ads.

items.summary: Busy mothers on both sides of the Atlantic are paying companies to handle their to-do lists.
items.body: Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores. Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it. "I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media. Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry. Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

items.title: Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback
items.summary: The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.
items.body: Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter. Dell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue. The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand. The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD . ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue.

items.title: World Cup drove profits surge, says Marston's

items.body: Pub company Marston's has said an "excellent World Cup" helped drive stronger trading as annual profits rose by nearly a fifth, despite reporting a dip in sales . The Wolverhampton-based firm, which operates more than 1,300 pubs across the UK, reported underlying pre-tax profits of £85.4m for the year to 26 September, up 18.4% from a year earlier. The company said trading was improved by new-look pubs, strong trade during this summer's football World Cup, and a partnership with Jeremy Clarkson's Hawkstone drinks brand. "For the third year running, profit is significantly up, cash flow is strong and margins have improved," said chief executive Justin Platt. The pub chain also said bookings for Christmas events were 9% ahead of the same point last year. Marston's has invested heavily in refurbishing pubs into new formats, including its sports-focused "Grandstand" venues.

items.body: Want to avoid the Christmas shopping hordes? Then let your AI agent do the shopping for you. Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app stores, having been downloaded millions of times. However, UK regulators have said they are keeping a close eye on the launch over privacy and consumer protection requirements. Muse can be used as an app or directly within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. Meta invites users to give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, so they can talk to it as well as assign it tasks such as sending an email, booking travel or buying festive presents.

items.body: Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington. As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around." Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top. items.title: The shake-up facing renters as a new kind of landlord emerges
items.summary: Companies building flats that they then rent out could usher in big changes for renters.
items.body: On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out. Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason. Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children. The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market - individuals who owned one or a handful of properties. Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed.

items.body: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? T hat’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous.

items.body: The tech billionaires could hardly contain their delight. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, in a one-word post on X. “Thanksgiving”, said Travis Kalanick, the Uber founder, who had been part of a core group of Silicon Valley leaders campaigning for this moment. “It is done,” intoned the world’s richest person, Elon Musk. “The mistake has been corrected.” Jensen Huang’s brief walk in the wilderness was over after being cast out of techland over his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Just 11 days after one of the most dramatic falls from grace in corporate history and just in time for the stock market to open on Wall Street on Monday, the chief executive of the US AI chip maker Nvidia, one of the richest people in the world and the avatar of the global AI boom, was back at the helm of his multitrillion-dollar empire.

items.body: W hen voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first , council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax. Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan . Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”.

items.summary: Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive…
items.body: Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view. Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang , was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race. The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

items.body: One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board reinstated Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy. But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward Folarin Balogun after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire. items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.summary: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist…
items.body: D uring the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK.

items.body: Jensen Huang has the backing of U.S. President Donald Trump and investors: Nvidia 's stock gained nearly $1 trillion after the abrupt board reversal that reinstated him as CEO. But investigations and governance questions still hang over the chipmaker, and analysts said that internal and external probes of Huang and Nvidia could fuel uncertainty. Trump's intervention to have Huang reinstated, alongside a concerted campaign from investors and employees, saw the Nvidia co-founder return just 11 days after he resigned amid reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. It was a dramatic turnaround just days after Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, rejected calls to reinstate Huang on Nov. 17.

items.body: G rounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly. Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure. In remarks consistent with previous statements , the influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 before hitting the goal the following year. He also said that while artificial intelligence is pressuring prices, there's "little evidence" it will be the source of more persistent inflation. items.body: U.S. Treasury yields were steady on Tuesday as investors looked ahead to more economic data releases due out later in the week. The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, student loans and credit card debt — was up more than 1 basis point at 4.932%. The 2-year Treasury note yield , the most sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was higher by more than 2 basis points at 4.691%. The 30-year Treasury yield — which often reacts the most to geopolitical developments — rose 2 basis points to 5.315%. The October reading of the personal consumption expenditures price index, which measures underlying inflation, is due Wednesday. A rise of 0.3% is expected, according to economists polled by Dow Jones, with the annual headline inflation anticipated to come in at 3.8%. The data comes after consumer confidence jumped in November.

items.body: A recent shopping trip to Morrisons cost me £100 in parking charges because its car park operator insists I never left. Euro Car Parks (ECP) claims my car remained there continuously for more than 13 hours because its ANPR cameras seemingly missed the first exit and the second entry. A fair few, according to online forums. You have fallen victim to what is known as “double-dipping”, when ANPR systems merge two separate parking sessions and generate a parking charge notice (PCN) for overstaying. You submitted bank statements showing that you were shopping or filling up with petrol in other distant locations during those 13 hours. Could it be coincidence that your PCN was cancelled two days after I contacted ECP and Morrisons? Morrisons tells me it had arranged for the charge to be cancelled and issued 10,000 More card points in goodwill. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually.

items.body: Jensen Huang 's return as Nvidia CEO may have eased concerns over the chipmaker's leadership, but it has also brought renewed scrutiny to the company's corporate governance and its reliance on its founder. Huang's abrupt departure and unexpected reinstatement exposed a deeper vulnerability at the heart of Nvidia, industry experts told CNBC, raising questions about board oversight and succession planning. "What does it mean if you have a company too big to fail or a CEO too big to fire?" Angela Mancini, head of advisory for global risk insights at Dow Jones, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia " on Tuesday. Mancini pointed to Huang's unusually large number of direct reports as another sign of how heavily Nvidia depends on its founder. "What does it mean when someone has 60 direct reports, and you literally are in a situation where you feel like you can't fire them?" she added.
